hints: Count carbon atoms in 2-bromopropane and in 2-methylpropylamine to work out whether the carbon skeleton grows during reaction 2 and reaction 3.
walkthrough:
Compare the carbon skeletons**
Look closely at the two ends. 2-bromopropane, $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CHBr}$, has 3 carbons. 2-methylpropylamine, $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{NH}_2$, has 4 carbons. So reaction 2 must add one extra carbon, and reaction 3 must turn that new carbon group into $\text{-CH}_2\text{NH}_2$.

Spot the classic one carbon extension**
The standard way to add exactly one carbon to a halogenoalkane and then make a primary amine with one extra $\text{CH}_2$ is through a nitrile. Reaction 2 substitutes $\text{-Br}$ by $\text{-CN}$, giving $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CHCN}$, 2-methylpropanenitrile. Reduction in reaction 3 then gives the amine.

hints: Think about what nucleophile replaces Br directly to give a primary amine with the same carbon skeleton in reaction 1.
Recall which nucleophile replaces a halogen by -CN and adds one carbon, and what solvent and heating it needs.
Recall the two standard reducing agents that convert a nitrile $\text{-C}\equiv\text{N}$ into a primary amine $\text{-CH}_2\text{NH}_2$.
walkthrough:
Reaction 1 keeps the same skeleton**
Methylethylamine, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(NH}_2\text{)CH}_3$, has the same 3 carbons as 2-bromopropane. This is direct nucleophilic substitution of $\text{Br}$ by $\text{NH}_3$. Use excess $\text{NH}_3$ in ethanol, heated under pressure or in a sealed tube to prevent loss of the volatile ammonia and to favour substitution.

Reaction 2 adds one carbon**
To make X, $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CHCN}$, you need cyanide as the nucleophile: $\text{KCN}$ or $\text{NaCN}$ dissolved in ethanol, heated under reflux. Ethanol is used because the halogenoalkane does not dissolve well in water, and heating speeds up substitution. The equation is $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CHBr} + \text{CN}^- \rightarrow \text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CHCN} + \text{Br}^-$.

Reaction 3 reduces the nitrile**
A nitrile is reduced to a primary amine with two added hydrogens on the nitrile carbon: $\text{-C}\equiv\text{N} \rightarrow \text{-CH}_2\text{NH}_2$. The two A Level reagents are hydrogen with a nickel catalyst, $\text{H}_2$ / Ni, or lithium aluminium hydride, $\text{LiAlH}_4$. Both deliver hydride / hydrogen to the electrophilic nitrile carbon.

Final answer: reaction 1: $\text{NH}_3$ in ethanol, heat under pressure or heat in a sealed tube
reaction 2: $\text{KCN}$ or $\text{NaCN}$ in ethanol, heat / reflux
reaction 3: $\text{H}_2$ with Ni catalyst or $\text{LiAlH}_4$

hints: Remember that an amine acts as a base by using its nitrogen lone pair to take a proton from water, leaving another ion behind.
walkthrough:
See the amine as a proton acceptor**
Ethylamine has a lone pair on nitrogen. In water it removes a proton, $\text{H}^+$, from a water molecule: $$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_3^+ + \text{OH}^-$$ The $\text{OH}^-$ produced makes the solution alkaline.

hints: Compare the groups attached to nitrogen in $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ and in $\text{NH}_3$ and think about whether ethyl pushes electrons toward nitrogen or away.
Link that electron push to how easily the nitrogen lone pair can be donated to a proton, $\text{H}^+$.
walkthrough:
Compare the structures**
Ammonia is $\text{NH}_3$ with three H atoms on N. Ethylamine is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ with an ethyl group in place of one H. Alkyl groups push electron density toward the atom they are attached to. This is the positive inductive effect.

Link electron density to basicity**
Basicity means ability to donate the nitrogen lone pair to a proton, $\text{H}^+$. The electron-donating ethyl group increases electron density on nitrogen, so the lone pair on ethylamine is more available than the lone pair on ammonia. Ethylamine therefore accepts $\text{H}^+$ more readily and is the stronger base.

Final answer: Ethylamine is more basic than ammonia.
The ethyl / alkyl group is electron-donating, which increases electron density on N and makes the lone pair more available for donation to / acceptance of $\text{H}^+$.

hints: Focus on what happens to pH when a small amount of acid or alkali is added to a buffer compared with pure water.
walkthrough:
Picture the key property**
Pure water changes pH dramatically with one drop of acid or alkali. A buffer does the opposite. It contains a reservoir of weak base and conjugate acid that mop up added $\text{H}^+$ or $\text{OH}^-$, so the pH stays almost constant when small amounts of acid or base are added.
Final answer: A solution which resists / minimises change in pH when small amounts of $\text{H}^+$ or $\text{OH}^-$ are added.

hints: Identify which component of the $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$ / $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_3\text{Cl}$ mixture will react with added $\text{H}^+$ ions.
Identify which component will react with added $\text{OH}^-$ ions and what neutral products it forms.
walkthrough:
Remove added acid with the free amine**
The mixture contains a large reserve of the weak base $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$. Added $\text{H}^+$ is accepted by the lone pair: $$\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2 + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{NH}_3^+$$ So $\text{H}^+$ is removed as the conjugate acid.

Remove added alkali with the conjugate acid**
The mixture also contains a large reserve of $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_3^+$, from $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_3\text{Cl}$. Added $\text{OH}^-$ reacts with it to reform the weak base: $$\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_3^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ So $\text{OH}^-$ is removed as water, and pH barely changes.

Final answer: For added acid: $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2 + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{NH}_3^+$
For added alkali: $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_3^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$ (accept $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_3\text{Cl} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{Cl}^-$)
